summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland operates by self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar, with no surgery and no court proceeding. Within the first months of the route about 350 people had used it. For under-18s the National Council removed the parental-consent requirement while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is still needed.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the 'Marriage for All' reform, which also opened adoption and IVF to same-sex couples; the reform was approved by 64.1% of voters in referendum.

Public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been punishable under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. That provision does not extend to gender identity, so a person targeted specifically for being trans does not receive the criminal-law aggravation available on sexual-orientation grounds. The Criminal Code contains no general hate-crime provision; offences are addressed through the anti-discrimination route instead.

Recorded anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime is rising: the LGBTIQ Helpline monitors roughly six reported incidents per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. International monitoring notes that Switzerland's recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes and that police do not record bias motivation, so official figures understate motivated violence.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022, according to UNHCR Switzerland's rights overview. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map rates Switzerland per category after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes.

At work, employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Articles 328ff of the Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act; trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.

Placement of trans people in detention is cantonal rather than federal: there is no federal provision, no Swiss case law on the subject, and no special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice. The canton of Basel-Stadt adopted its detention law (JVG) on 13 November 2019, whose separation rules require female and male detainees to be held separately and state that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate able to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.
tangentialFactors:
Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions, but the bill is still pending in the Council of States. Cantonal bans are in force in Neuchâtel from 2023 and in Valais and Vaud from 2024. The Federal Council states that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them and would breach professional duties; a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open.

Blood donation rules moved on 1 November 2023 to a four-month deferral after last sexual contact for gay men, down from the one-year deferral in force since 2017.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page records Switzerland's overall index score and per-category compliance ratings, assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes; the inventory does not state the numeric score itself. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Switzerland records that the country reports hate-crime data regularly while noting the recording weaknesses described above.

LegalClarity's assessment of 3 June 2026 frames the Swiss position as running from marriage equality to gender recognition with some gaps remaining, a description consistent with the missing gender-identity coverage in Article 261bis.
localsOnly:
Support infrastructure includes a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland advising on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum.

A 2018 survey of 1,700 Neuchâtel schoolchildren aged 14 and 15 found that 10% of girls and 5% of boys identified as LGBT; 38% reported receiving slaps, kicks or punches, 25% reported frequent harassment, 16% reported being a victim of physical violence, and 7% reported discrimination by a teacher. Since the mid-1990s an annual Coming Out Day has been observed in schools, high schools and universities, often via seminars, films and group discussion, and LGBT youth groups operate at EPFL, ETH Zurich, Lausanne and St. Gallen.

Workplace protection is enforced through the Code of Obligations and the Equality Act, and trans employees do not need an amended civil register entry to be addressed by their chosen name and gender at work.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Article 261bis will be extended to cover gender identity is not addressed in the sources, and no pending legislative proposal on that point is recorded.

Unresolved: the sources state that placement of trans detainees is cantonal and that no federal rule or case law exists, so the practice a visitor would actually encounter varies by canton and is only documented here for Basel-Stadt.

Unresolved: the numerical ILGA-Europe index score for Switzerland is referenced but not supplied in the inventory.

Unresolved: the OSCE/ODIHR observation that police do not record bias motivation means the true level of anti-trans violence in Switzerland cannot be verified from official statistics; the figure of roughly six incidents per week derives from helpline monitoring rather than police recording.
